transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
A federal judge has thrown out the Trump administration's highly unusual lawsuit over the U.S. Senate race in Alaska.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang reports the administration plans to appeal the ruling.
The Trump administration asked the judge to block the certification of results from the U.S. Senate race in Alaska
if the Republican incumbent loses.
But U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason found the administration does not have the ability to bring this lawsuit.
President Trump said he ordered it to be filed because out of the four Senate candidates on Alaska's ballot,
two have similar names, the Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan
and Daniel Sullivan Jr., who is not affiliated with a local party.
In June, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled Daniel Sullivan Jr. has the right to run as a candidate.
A recent New York Times report that NPR has not independently confirmed
says Democratic campaign operatives were behind efforts to prop up Sullivan Jr. as a spoiler candidate.
The Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, has denied any involvement.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
In Michigan, Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost a close Senate primary to Abdul Al Sayed,
is breaking with her party and endorsing Republican Mike Rogers instead.
This two days before the midterm elections on Tuesday.
She endorsed Rogers after she was uninvited to a joint event with Al Sayed.
Stevens has been critical of Al Sayed's comments on Israel, but recently said she would vote for him.
Al Sayed on the campaign trail spoke to reporters after Stevens' decision saying he doesn't think about her.
My focus has never wavered.
I have been clear about what our responsibilities are.
So rather than focus on a distraction about who said what to whom, where they went, I've been consistent.
I want to get money out of politics.
I want to put money back in pockets.
Michigan is a key battleground in Tuesday's midterms with critical House and Senate races that could decide control of Congress.
Democrats need to net just four Senate seats around the country to reclaim that chamber.
Affordable Health Care Act enrollment for health insurance started in most states today with new rules and higher costs for some.
And Pierre Chantaliz Duster has more.
Some enrollees will have to navigate new changes, including verifying their identity or using a confirmation code.
Those deemed high risk must have their identity verified by a third party company such as Experian.
Enrollment is expected to be lower this year after enhanced subsidies expired at the end of 2025.
This means some will face significantly higher premiums.
Some people enrolled in Obamacare will receive a subsidy, but it will be a lower amount.
Medical care costs, labor shortages and inflation are also contributing to higher costs.
The enrollment period lasts through January 15th.
Chantaliz Duster, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
A federal judge is refusing to dismiss a lawsuit that claims McDonald's is defrauding its customers.
And Pierre Chantaliz Duster reports the dispute is over its popular McRib sandwich.
The proposed class action lawsuit will be allowed to proceed following the ruling by U.S. District Judge April Perry.
While she did throw out some claims, she said it was too soon to accept McDonald's argument that no reasonable consumer would expect the McRib to be made from rib meat.
Four plaintiffs are suing McDonald's, claiming the company is trying to fool customers by shaping their meat to look like ribs,
when in fact they say it's made from pork shoulder, heart, tripe or stomach meat.
They say the use of lower quality meat means consumers are being overcharged for the $7 sandwich.
McDonald's denies they use hearts, tripe or stomach meat in the McRib and says their marketing is not deceptive.
John Stolness, NPR News.
After a failed rescue effort left it sinking lower and lower, a NASA telescope is now wobbling in space.
And officials say it is expected to come crashing down at the end of the week,
although most of the one and a half ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere.
But NASA says some of it could survive reentry.
The space agency says intense solar activity dragged it down faster than expected.
That prompted NASA to stage a $30 million rescue mission.
The Swift Observatory says some of the universe's biggest explosions happened during the telescope's 22 years in orbit.
You're listening to NPR News.

topics.text: Federal judge throws out Trump administration's lawsuit over Alaska Senate race certification
Michigan Congresswoman Haley Stevens breaks with party, endorses Republican Mike Rogers for Senate
Affordable Care Act enrollment opens with new identity verification rules and higher costs for some
Federal judge refuses to dismiss proposed class action accusing McDonald's of misleading McRib meat claims
NASA's wobbling Swift telescope expected to fall to Earth at week's end, with some debris surviving
